entities.summary:
Domenico Rosselli, an Italian sculptor active during the late Quattrocento, played a significant role in the vibrant artistic landscape of Florence, contributing to the decorative and architectural sculpture of the early Renaissance. Though not as widely celebrated as contemporaries like Michelangelo or Donatello, Rosselli's prolific workshop produced numerous works, primarily in marble and stucco, that defined the aesthetic sensibilities of wealthy patrons and religious institutions in Tuscany. His artistic output, spanning from approximately the 1470s until his death in 1498, reflects the evolving tastes and technical advancements of the period, particularly in relief sculpture and portrait busts.

Rosselli's core contributions lie in his mastery of detailed, often narrative, relief work and his adept use of stucco, a medium that allowed for more economical and widespread dissemination of fashionable designs. He is credited with several funerary monuments and decorative elements within Florentine palaces and churches, including the elegant marble altar in the Baroncelli Chapel in Santa Croce, which exemplifies his refined classical style and meticulous craftsmanship. His workshop also produced a considerable number of Madonna and Child reliefs, often incorporating innovative compositional elements that influenced other local sculptors and painters. Rosselli's collaboration with architects and painters was common, integrating his sculptural forms into larger decorative schemes.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Domenico Rosselli was a significant regional sculptor whose workshop contributed substantially to the decorative arts and visual culture of late 15th-century Florence, influencing local artistic trends and transmitting key techniques. His works helped define the aesthetic of the Florentine Renaissance for a broad range of patrons.
